title: switch
learningObjectives: Explain switch and choose an appropriate control-flow structure.

understand.concept: The switch statement compares an expression with case values using strict equality. break exits the switch; without it, execution can fall through to subsequent cases. default handles unmatched values.
understand.whyItMatters: switch can make multiple exact-value branches readable. For range checks or complex boolean conditions, if/else may be clearer.
understand.analogy: switch is like a labelled set of choices where the matching label selects a path.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; JavaScript control flow follows precise condition evaluation and iteration semantics.

explain.narrative: The Tuesday case matches and prints Build. break prevents fall-through into default.

examples.explanation: The Tuesday case matches and prints Build. break prevents fall-through into default.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser console displays the sequence or branch results described.

practise.guidedTask: Create a switch for three course states and a default. Remove one break deliberately and observe fall-through.
practise.independentTask: Write a small program that uses the control-flow structure to process learner or course data. Test normal, boundary, and empty cases.
hints: Use strict comparisons for exact values.
Choose for...of for iterable values and avoid confusing keys with values.

practice.starterCode:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>switch</title></head><body>
<script>const day='Tuesday';switch(day){case 'Monday':console.log('Plan');break;case 'Tuesday':console.log('Build');break;default:console.log('Review');}</script>
</body></html>

questions.prompt: What does break do in a switch statement?
questions.explanation: break prevents execution from falling through to later case clauses.
